speeches.speaker: An.
verse: HEART, wilt not break! & thou abhorred life
Wilt thou still breath in my enraged bloud?
Vaines, synewes, arteries, why crack yee not?
Burst and diuul'st, with anguish of my griefe.
Can man by no meanes creepe out of himselfe,
And leaue the slough of viperous griefe behinde?
Antonio, hast thou seene a fight at sea,
As horrid as the hideous day of doome;
Betwixt thy father, duke of Genoa,
And proud Piero, the Venetian Prince?
In which the sea hath swolne with Genoas bloud,
And made spring tydes with the warme reeking gore,
That gusht from out our Gallies scupper holes;
In which, thy father, poore Andrugio,
Lyes sunk, or leapt into the armes of chaunce,
Choakt with the laboring Oceans brackish fome;
Who euen, despite Pieros can cred hate,
Would with an armed hand haue seiz'd thy loue,
And linkt thee to the beautious Mellida.
Haue I outliu'd the death of all these hopes?
Haue I felt anguish pourd into my heart,
Burning like Balsamum in tender wounds;
And yet dost liue! could not the fretting sea
Haue rowl'd me vp in wrinkles of his browe?
Is death growen coy? or grim confusion nice?
That it will not accompany a wretch,
But I must needs be cast on Venice shoare?
And try new fortunes with this strange disguise?
To purchase my adored Mellida.
Harke how Piero's triumphs beat the ayre,
O rugged mischiefe how thou grat'st my heart!
Take spirit, blood, disguise, be confident:
Make a firme stand, here rests the hope of all,
Lower then hell, there is no depth to fall.

speeches.speaker: Piero.
verse: Victorious Fortune, with tryumphant hand,
Hurleth my glory 'bout this ball of earth,
Whil'st the Venetian Duke is heaued vp
On wings of faire successe, to ouer-looke
The low cast ruines of his enemies,
To see my selfe ador'd, and Genoa quake,
My fate is firmer then mischance can shake.

speeches.speaker: Feli.
verse: Stand, the ground trembleth.

speeches.speaker: Piero.
verse: Hah? an earthquake?

speeches.speaker: Ball.
verse: Oh, I smell a sound.

speeches.speaker: Feli.
verse: Piero stay, for I descry a fume,
Creeping from out the bosome of the deepe,
The breath of darkenesse, fatall when 'tis whist
In greatnes stomacke: this same smoake, call'd pride,
Take heede shee'le lift thee to improuidence,
And breake thy necke from steepe securitie,
Shee'le make thee grudge to let Iehoua share
In thy successefull battailes: O, shee's ominous,
Inticeth princes to deuour heauen,
Swallow omnipotence, out-stare dread fate,
Subdue Eternitie in giant thought,
Heaues vp their hurt with swelling, puft conceit,
Till their soules burst with venom'd Arrogance:
Beware Piero, Rome it selfe hath tried,
Confusions traine blowes vp this Babell pride.

speeches.speaker: Pier.
verse: Pish, Dimitto superos, summa votorum attigi.
Alberto, hast thou yeelded vp our fixt decree
Vnto the Genoan Embassadour?
Are they content if that their duke returne,
To send his, and his sonne Antonios head,
As pledges steept in bloud, to gaine their peace?

speeches.speaker: Alb.
verse: With most obsequious, sleek-brow'd intertain,
They all embrace it as most gratious.

speeches.speaker: Pier.
verse: Are Proclamations sent through Italy,
That whosoeuer brings Andrugios head,
Oryoung Anthonios, shall be guerdoned
With twentie thousand double Pistolets,
And be indeened to Pieros loue?

speeches.speaker: Forob.
verse: They are sent euery way: sound policy.
Sweete Lord.

speeches.speaker: Fel.
verse: Confusion to these limber Sycophants.
No sooner mischief's borne in regenty,
But flattery christens it with pollicy.
VVhy then: O me Celitum excelsissimum!
The intestine malice, and inueterate hate
I alwaies bore to that Andrugio,
Glories in triumph ore his misery:
Nor shall that carpet-boy Antonio
Match with my daughter, sweet cheekt Mellida.
No, the publick power makes my faction strong.

speeches.speaker: Fel.
verse: Ill, when publick power stre~gthneth priuate wro~g.

speeches.speaker: Pie.
verse: Tis horse-like, not for man, to know his force.

speeches.speaker: Fel.
verse: Tis god-like, for a man to feele remorse.

speeches.speaker: Pie.
verse: Pish, I prosecute my families reuenge,
VVhich Ile pursue with such a burning chace
Till I haue dri'd vp all Andrugios bloud;
VVeake rage, that with slight pittie is withstoode.
VVhat meanes that fresh triumphall florish sound?

speeches.speaker: Alb.
verse:
The prince of Millane, and young Florence heir
Approach to gratulate your victorie.

speeches.speaker: Pie.
verse: VVeele girt them with an ample waste of loue;
Conduct them to our presence royally.
Let vollies of the great Artillery
From of our gallies banks play prodigall,
And sou~d lowd welcome fro~ their bellowing mouths.

speeches.speaker: Mell.
verse:
VVhat prince was that passed through my fathers
guard?

speeches.speaker: Fla.
verse: Twas Galeatzo, the young Florentine.

speeches.speaker: Ros.
verse: Troth, one that will besiege thy maidenhead,
Enter the wals yfaith (sweet Mellida)
If that thy flankers be not Canon proofe.

speeches.speaker: Mell.
verse: Oh Mary Ambree, good, thy iudgement wench;
Thy bright electious cleere, what will he prooue?

speeches.speaker: Ross.
verse: Hath a short finger aud a naked chinne;
A skipping eye, dare lay my iudgement (faith)
His loue is glibbery; there's no hold ont, wench:
Giue me a husband whose aspect is firme,
A full cheekt gallant, with a bouncing thigh:
Oh, he is the Paradizo dell madonne contento.

speeches.speaker: Mell.
verse: Euen such a one was my Antonio.

speeches.speaker: Rossa.
verse: By my nine and thirteth seruant (sweete)
Thou art in loue, but stand on tiptoed faire,
Here comes Saint Tristram Tirlery whiffe yfaith.

speeches.speaker: Mell.
verse: S. Marke, S. Marke, what kind of thing appears?

speeches.speaker: Ross.
verse: For fancies passion, spit vpon him; figh:
His face is varnisht: in the name of loue,
VVhat country bred that creature?

speeches.speaker: Mell.
verse: VVhat is he Flauia?

speeches.speaker: Fla.
verse: The heire of Millane, Segnior Matzagent.

speeches.speaker: Ross.
verse: Matzagent? now by my pleasures hope,
He is made like a tilting staffe; and lookes
For all the world like an ore-rosted pigge:
A great Tobacco taker too, thats flat.
For his eyes looke as if they had bene hung
In the smoake of his nose.

speeches.speaker: Mell.
verse: What husband, wil he prooue sweete Rossaline?

speeches.speaker: Ross.
verse: Auoid him: for he hath a dwindled legge,
A lowe forehead, and a thinne cole-black beard,
And will be iealous too, beleeue it sweete:
For his chin sweats, and hath a gander neck,
A thinne lippe, and a little monkish eye:
Pretious, what a slender waste he hath!
He lookes like a May-pole, or a notched stick:
Heele snap in two at euery little straine.
Giue me a husband that will fill mine armes,
Of steddie iudgement, quicke and nimble sense:
Fooles relish not a Ladies excellence.

speeches.speaker: Mell.
verse: The tryumph's ended, but looke Rossaline,
What gloomy soule in strange accustrements
Walkes on the pauement.

speeches.speaker: Rossa.
verse: Good sweete lets to her, pree the Mellida.

speeches.speaker: Mell.
verse: How couetous thou art of nouelties!

speeches.speaker: Rossa.
verse: Pish, tis our nature to desire things
That are thought strangers to the common cut.

speeches.speaker: Mell.
verse: I am exceeding willing, but—

speeches.speaker: Ross.
verse: But what? pree the goe downe, lets see her face:
God send that neither wit nor beauty wants
Those tempting sweets, affections Adamants.

speeches.speaker: Anto.
verse: Come downe, she comes like: O, no Simile
Is pretious, choyce, or elegant enough
To illustrate her descent: leape heart, she comes,
She comes: smile heauen, and softest Southern winde
Kisse her cheeke gently with perfumed breath.
She comes: Creations puritie, admir'd.
Ador'd, amazing raritie, she comes.
O now Antonio presse thy spirit forth
In following passion, knit thy senses close,
Heape vp thy powers, double all thy man:
She comes. O how her eyes dart wonder on my heart!
Mount bloode, soule to my lips, tast Hebes cup:
Stand firme on decke, when beauties close fight's vp.

speeches.speaker: Mel.
verse: Ladie, your strange habit doth beget
Our pregnant thoughts, euen great of much desire,
To be acquaint with your condition.

speeches.speaker: Rossa.
verse: Good sweete Lady, without more ceremonies,
What country claims your birth, & sweet your name?

speeches.speaker: Anto.
verse: In hope your bountie will extend it selfe,
In selfe same nature of faire curtesie,
Ile shunne all nicenesse; my nam's Florizell,
My country Scythia, I am Amazon,
Cast on this shore by furie of the sea.

speeches.speaker: Ross.
verse: Nay faith, sweete creature, weele not vaile our names.
It pleas'd the Font to dip me Rossaline.
That Ladie beares the name of Mellida,
The duke of Venice daughter.

speeches.speaker: Anto.
verse: Madam, I am oblig'd to kisse your hand,
By imposition of a now dead man.

speeches.speaker: Rossa.
verse: Now by my troth, I long beyond all thought,
To know the man; sweet beauty deigne his name.

speeches.speaker: Anto.
verse: Ladie, the circumstance is tedious.

speeches.speaker: Ros.
verse: Troth not a whit; good faire, lets haue it all:
I loue not, I, to haue a iot left out,
If the tale come from a lou'd Orator.

speeches.speaker: Anto.
verse: Vouchsafe me then your hush't obseruances.
Vehement in pursuite of strange nouelties,
After long trauaile through the Asian maine,
I shipt my hopefull thoughts for Britany;
Longing to viewe great natures miracle,
The glorie of our sex, whose fame doth strike
Remotest eares with adoration.
Sayling some two monthes with inconstant winds,
We view'd the glistering Venetian forts;
To which we made: when loe, some three leagues off,
We might descry a horred spectacle:
The issue of black fury strow'd the sea,
With tattered carcasses of splitted ships,
Halfe sinking, burning, floating, topsie turuie.
Not farre from these sad ruines of fell rage,
We might behold a creature presse the waues;
Senselesse he sprauld, all notcht with gaping wounds:
To him we made, and (short) we tooke him vp:
The first word that he spake was, Mellida;
And then he swouned.

speeches.speaker: Mell.
verse: Aye me!

speeches.speaker: Anto.
verse: Why sigh you, faire?

speeches.speaker: Ross.
verse: Nothing but little humours: good sweet, on.

speeches.speaker: Anto.
verse: His wounds being drest, and life recouered,
We gan discourse; when loe, the sea grewe mad,
His bowels rumbling with winde passion,
Straightswarthy darknesse popt out Phoebus eye,
And blurd the iocund face of bright cheekt day;
Whilst crudl'd fogges masked euen darknesse brow:
Heauen bad's good night, and the rocks gron'd
At the intestine vprore of the maine.
Now gustie flawes strook vp the very heeles
Of our maine mast, whilst the keene lightning shot
Through the black bowels of the quaking ayte:
Straight chops a waue, and in his sliftred panch
Downe fals our ship, and there he breaks his neck:
Which in an instant vp was belkt againe.
VVhen thus this martyrd soule began to sigh;
" Giue me your hand (quoth he) now doe you graspe
" Th'vnequall mirrour of ragg'd misery:
" Is't not a horrid storme? O, well shap't sweete,
" Could your quicke eye strike through these gashed wou~ds,
" You should beholde a heart, a heart, faire creature,
" Raging more wilde then is this franticke sea.
" VVolt doe me a fauour, if thou chance suruiue?
" But visit Venice, kisse the pretious white
" Of my most; nay all all Epithites are base
" To attribute to gratious Mellida:
" Tell her the spirit of Antonio
" VVisheth his last gaspe breath'd vpon her breast.

speeches.speaker: Ros.
verse: VVhy weepes soft hearted Florisell?

speeches.speaker: Ant.
verse: Alas, the flintie rocks groand at his plaints.
Tell her (quoth he) that her obdurate sire
Hath crackt his bosome; therewithall he wept,
And thus sigh't on. The sea is merciful;
Looke how it gapes to bury all my griefe
Well, thou shalt haue it, thou shalt be his toumbe:
My faith in my loue liue; in thee, dy woe,
Dye vnmatcht anguish, dye Antonio:
With that he totterd from the reeling decke,
And downe he sunke.

speeches.speaker: Ross.
verse: Pleasures bodie, what makes my Lady weepe?

speeches.speaker: Mell.
verse: Nothing, sweet Rossaline, but the ayer's sharpe.
My fathers Palace, Madam, will be proud
To entertaine your presence, if youle daine
To make repose within. Aye me!

speeches.speaker: Ant.
verse: Ladie our fashion is not curious.

speeches.speaker: Ross.
verse: Faith all the nobler, tis more generous.

speeches.speaker: Mell.
verse: Shall I then know how fortune fell at last,
What succour came, or what strange fate insew'd?

speeches.speaker: Ant.
verse: Most willingly: but this same court is vast,
And publike to the staring multitude.

speeches.speaker: Rossa.
verse: Sweet Lady, nay good sweet, now by my troth
VVeele be bedfellowes: durt on complement froth.

speeches.speaker: Dil.
prose:
HAH Catzo, your master wants a cleane trencher:
doe you heare?

speeches.speaker: Balurdo
prose: cals for your diminutiue attendance.

speeches.speaker: Catz.
prose: The belly hath no eares Dildo.

speeches.speaker: Dil.
prose: Good pugge giue me some capon.

speeches.speaker: Catz.
prose:
No capon, no not a bitte yee smooth bully; capon's
no meat for Dildo: milke, milke, yee glibbery vrchin,
is foode for infants.

speeches.speaker: Dil.
prose: Vpon mine honour

speeches.speaker: Cat.
prose:
Your honour with a paugh? slid, now euery Iack
an Apes loads his backe with the golden coat of honour;
euery Asse puts on the Lyons skinne and roars
his honour, vpon your honour. By my Ladies pantable,
I feare I shall liue to heare a Vintners boy cry; tis
rich neat Canary, vpon my honour.

speeches.speaker: Dil.
prose: My stomack's vp.

speeches.speaker: Cat.
prose: I think thou art hungry.

speeches.speaker: Dil.
prose:
The match of furie is lighted, fastned to the linstock
of rage, and will presently set fire to the touchhole
of intemperance, discharging the double couluering
of my incensement in the face of thy opprobrious
speach.

speeches.speaker: Cat.
prose:
Ile stop the barrell thus; god Dildo, set not fire to
the touch-hole.

speeches.speaker: Dil.
prose:
My rage is stopt, and I wil eate to the health of
the foole thy master Castilio.

speeches.speaker: Cat.
prose:
And I will suck the iuyce of the capon, to the
health of the Idiot thy master Balurdo.

speeches.speaker: Dil.
prose:
Faith, our masters are like a case of Rapiers sheathed
in one scabberd of folly.

speeches.speaker: Cat.
prose:
Right dutch blades. But was't not rare sport at
the sea-battle, whilst rounce robble hobble roard from
the ship sides, to viewe our masters pluck their plumes
and droppe their feathers, for feare of being men of
marke.

speeches.speaker: Dill.
prose:
Slud (cri'd Signior Balurdo) O for Don Bessiclers
armour, in the Mirror of Knighthood: what coil's here?
O for an armour, Canon proofe: O, more cable, more
fetherbeds, more fetherbeds, more cable, till hee had
as much as my cable hatband, to fence him.

speeches.speaker: Catz.
prose: Buxome Flauia: can you sing? song, song.

speeches.speaker: Fla.
prose:
My sweete Dildo, I am not for you at this time:
Madam Rossaline stayes for a fresh ruffe to appeare in
the presence: sweete away.

speeches.speaker: Dil.
prose:
Twill not be so put off, delicate, delicious, spark
eyed, sleek skind, sle~der wasted, clean legd, rarely shap't.

speeches.speaker: Fla.
prose:
VVho, Ile be at all your seruice another season:
nay faith ther's reason in all things.

speeches.speaker: Dil.
prose:
VVould I were reason then, that I might be in
all things.

speeches.speaker: Cat.
prose:
The breefe and the semiquauer is, wee must
haue the descant you made vpon our names, ere you
depart.

speeches.speaker: Fla.
prose: Faith, the song will seeme to come off hardly.

speeches.speaker: Catz.
prose:
Troth not a whit, if you seeme to come off
quickly.

speeches.speaker: Fla.
prose: Peart Catzo, knock it lustily then.

speeches.speaker: Foro.
prose:
Make place gentlemen; pages, hold torches,
the prince approacheth the presence.

speeches.speaker: Dill.
prose:
VVhat squeaking cart-wheel haue we here? ha?

Make place gentlemen, pages holde torches, the
prince approacheth the presence.

speeches.speaker: Ros.
prose:
Faugh, what a strong sent's here, some bodie
vseth to weare socks.

speeches.speaker: Bal.
prose:
By this faire candle light, tis not my feete, I neuer
wore socks since I suckt pappe.

speeches.speaker: Ross.
prose: Sauourly put off.

speeches.speaker: Cast.
prose:
Hah, her wit stings, blisters, galles off the skinne
with the tart acrimony of her sharpe quicknesse: by
sweetenesse, she is the very Pallas that flewe out of Iupiters
brainepan. Delicious creature, vouchsafe mee
your seruice: by the puritie of bounty, I shall be proud
of such bondage.

speeches.speaker: Ross.
prose:
I vouchsafe it; be my slaue. Signior Balurdo, wilt
thou be my seruant too?

speeches.speaker: Ba.
prose:
O god: forsooth in very good earnest, law, you wold
make me as a man should say, as a man should say.

speeches.speaker: Fe.
prose: Slud sweet beauty, will you deign him your seruice?

speeches.speaker: Ros.
prose:
O, your foole is your only seruant. But good Feliche
why art thou so sad? a pennie for thy thought, ma~.

speeches.speaker: Feli.
prose:
I sell not my thought so cheap: I valewe my
meditation at a higher rate.

speeches.speaker: Ball.
prose:
In good sober sadnesse, sweet mistris, you should
haue had my thought for a penny: by this crimson Satten
that cost eleuen shillings, thirteene pence, three
pence, halfe pennie a yard, that you should, law.

speeches.speaker: Ros.
prose: VVhat was thy thought, good seruant?

speeches.speaker: Ba.
prose:
Marrie forsooth, hovv manie strike of pease would
feed a hog far against Christide.

speeches.speaker: ^o.
prose: Paugh; seruant rub out my rheum, it soiles the presence.

speeches.speaker: Casti.
prose:
By my wealthiest thought, you grace my shoo
with an vnmeasured honour: I will preserue the soale
of it, as a most sacred relique, for this seruice.

speeches.speaker: Ross.
prose:
Ile spit in thy mouth, and thou wilt, to grace
thee.

speeches.speaker: Felich.
verse: O that the stomack of this queasie age
Digestes, or brookes such raw vnseasoned gobs,
And vomits not them forth! O slauish sots.
Seruant quoth you? faugh: if a dogge should craue
And beg her seruice, he should haue it straight:
Sheed giue him fauours too; to lick her feete,
Or fetch her fanne, or some such drudgery:
A good dogs office, which these amorists
Tryumph of: tis rare, well giue her more Asse,
More sot, as long as dropping of her nose
Is sworne rich pearle by such low slaues as those.

speeches.speaker: Ross.
verse: Flauia, attend me to attire me.

speeches.speaker: Balur.
prose:
In sad good earnest, sir, you haue toucht the
very bare of naked truth; my silk stocking hath a good
glosse, and I thanke my planets, my legge is not altogether
vnpropitiously shap't. There's a word: vnpropitiously?
I thinke I shall speake vnpropitiously as well
as any courtier in Italy.

speeches.speaker: Foro.
prose:
So helpe me your sweete bounty, you haue the
most gracefull presence, applasiue elecuty, amazing
volubility, polisht adornation, delicious affabilitie.

speeches.speaker: Fel.
prose:
Whop: fut how he tickles yon trout vnder the
gilles! you shall see him take him by and by, with groping
flattery.

speeches.speaker: Foro.
prose:
That euer rauisht the eare of wonder. By
your sweete selfe, then whome I knowe not a more
exquisite, illustrate, accomplished, pure, respected, ador'd,
obserued, pretious, reall, magnanimous, bou~
tious:
if you haue an idle rich cast ierkin, or so, it shall
not be cast away, if; hah? heres a foreheade, an eye,
a heade, a haire, that would make a: or if you haue any
spare paire of siluer spurs, ile doe you as much
right in all kinde offices

speeches.speaker: Fel.
prose: Of a kinde Parasite

speeches.speaker: Foro.
prose: As any of my meane fortunes shall be able to

speeches.speaker: Balur.
prose:
As I am true Christian now, thou hast wonne
the spurres

speeches.speaker: Feli.
verse: For flattery.
O how I hate that same Egyptian louse;
A rotten maggot, that liues by stinking filth
Of tainted spirits: vengeance to such dogs,
That sprout by gnawing senselesse carion.

speeches.speaker: Alb.
prose: Gallants, saw you my mistresse, the Ladie Rossaline?

speeches.speaker: Foro.
prose:
My mistresse, the Ladie Rossaline, left the presence
euen now.

speeches.speaker: Casti.
prose:
My mistresse, the Ladie Rossaline, withdrewe
her gratious aspect euen now.

speeches.speaker: Balur.
prose:
My mistresse, the Ladie Rossaline, withdrewe
her gratious aspect euen now.

speeches.speaker: Felich.
prose: Well said eccho.

speeches.speaker: Alb.
verse: Alberto liues, to haue such riuals.
Slid, I haue bin searching euery priuate rome,
Corner, and secret angle of the court:
And yet, and yet, and yet she liues conceal'd.
Good sweete Feliche, tell me how to finde
My bright fac't mistresse out.
prose:
My mistresse, and his mistresse, and your mistresse,
& the dogs mistresse: pretious dear heauen, that

speeches.speaker: Fel.
prose:
Why man, cry out for lanthorne and candlelight.
For tis your onely way, to finde your bright flaming
wench, with your light burning torch: for most
commonly, these light creatures liue in darknesse.

speeches.speaker: Alb.
prose: Away you heretike, youle be burnt for

speeches.speaker: Fel.
prose:
Goe, you amorous hound, follow the sent of
your mistresse shooe; away.

speeches.speaker: Foro.
prose:
Make a faire presence, boyes, aduance your
lightes:
The Princesse makes approach.

speeches.speaker: Bal.
prose:
And please the gods, now in very good deede,
law, you shal see me tickle the measures for the heaue~s,
Doe my hangers showe?

speeches.speaker: Pie.
verse: Beautious Amazon, sit, and seat your thoughts
In the reposure of most soft content.
Sound musick there. Nay daughter, cleare your eyes,
From these dull fogs of mistie discontent:
Look sprightly girl. What? though Antonio's droun'd,
That peeuish dotard on thy excellence,
That hated issue of Andrugio:
Yet maist thou tryumph in my victories;
Since, loe, the high borne bloodes of Italy
Sue for thy seate of loue.
Beautie and youth run descant on loues ground.

speeches.speaker: Matz.
verse: Ladie, erect your gratious summetry:
Shine in the spheare of sweete affection:
Your eye as heauie, as the heart of night.

speeches.speaker: Mell.
prose:
My thoughts are as black as your bearde, my
fortunes as ill proportioned as your legs; and all the
powers of my minde, as leaden as your wit, and as
dustie as your face is swarthy.

speeches.speaker: Gal.
verse: Faith sweet, ile lay thee on the lips for that iest.

speeches.speaker: Mell.
verse: I pree thee intrude not on a dead mans right.

speeches.speaker: Gal.
verse: No, but the liuings iust possession.
Thy lips, and loue, are mine.

speeches.speaker: Mell.
verse: You nere tooke seizin on them yet: forbeare:
There's not a vacant corner of my heart,
But all is fild with deade Antonios losse.
Then vrge no more; O leaue to loue at all;
Tis lesse disgracefull, not to mount, then fall.

speeches.speaker: Mat.
verse: Bright and refulgent Ladie, daine your eare:
You see this blade, had it a courtly lip,
It would diuulge my valour, plead my loue,
Iustle that skipping feeble amorist
Out of your loues seat; I am Matzagent.

speeches.speaker: Gale.
verse: Harke thee, I pray thee taint not thy sweete eare
With that sots gabble; By thy beautious cheeke,
He is the flagging'st bulrush that ere droopt
With each slight mist of raine. But with pleas'd eye
Smile on my courtshippe.

speeches.speaker: Mel.
verse: What said you sir? alas my thought was fixt
Vpon another obiect. Good, forbeare:
I shall but weepe. Aye me, what bootes a teare!
Come, come, lets daunce. O musicke thou distill'st
More sweetnesse in vs then this iarring world:
Both time and measure from thy straines doe breath,
Whilst from the channell of this durt doth flowe
Nothing but timelesse griefe, vnmeasured woe.

speeches.speaker: Anto.
verse: O how impatience cramps my cracked veins,
And cruddles thicke my blood, with boiling rage!
O eyes, why leape you not like thunderbolts,
Or canon bullets in my riuals face;
Oy me infeliche misero, o lamenteuol fato!

speeches.speaker: Alber.
verse: What meanes the Lady fal vpon the grou~d?

speeches.speaker: Ross.
verse: Belike the falling sicknesse.

speeches.speaker: Anto.
verse: I cannot brooke this sight, my thoughts grow wilde:
Here lies a wretch, on whome heauen neuer smilde.

speeches.speaker: Ross.
verse: What seruant, nere a word, and I here man?
I would shoot some speach forth, to strike the time
With pleasing touch of amorous complement.
Say sweete, what keepes thy minde, what think'st thou

speeches.speaker: Alb.
verse: Nothing. on?

speeches.speaker: Rossa.
verse: Whats that nothing?

speeches.speaker: Alb.
verse: A womans constancie.

speeches.speaker: Rossa.
prose:
Good, why, would'st thou haue vs sluts, & neuer
shift the vestur of our thoughts? Away for shame.

speeches.speaker: Alb.
verse: O no, thart too constant to afflict my heart,
Too too firme fixed in vnmooued scorne.

speeches.speaker: Ross.
verse: Pish, pish; I fixed in vnmooued scorne?
Why, Ile loue thee to night.

speeches.speaker: Alb.
verse: But whome to morrow?

speeches.speaker: Ross.
verse: Faith, as the toy puts me in the head.

speeches.speaker: Bal.
prose:
And pleased the marble heauens, now would I
might be the toy, to put you in the head, kindly to conceipt
my my my: pray you giue in an Epithite for loue.

speeches.speaker: Fel.
prose: Roaring, roaring.

O loue thou hast murdred me, made me a shadowe,
and you heare not Balurdo, but Balurdos ghost.

speeches.speaker: Rossa.
prose: Can a ghost speake?

speeches.speaker: Bal.
prose: Scuruily, as I doe.

speeches.speaker: Ross.
prose: And walke?

speeches.speaker: Bal.
prose: After their fashion.

speeches.speaker: Ross.
prose: And eate apples?

speeches.speaker: Bal.
prose: In a sort, in their garbe.

speeches.speaker: Feli.
prose: Pree thee Flauia be my mistresse.

speeches.speaker: Fla.
prose: Your reason, good Feliche?

speeches.speaker: Fel.
prose:
Faith, I haue nineteene mistresses alreadie, and I
not much disdeigne that thou shold'st make vp the ful
score.

speeches.speaker: Fla.
prose:
Oh, I heare you make common places of your
mistresses, to performe the office of memory by. Pray
you, in auncient times were not those satten hose? In
good faith, now they are new dyed, pinkt & scoured,

they showe as well as if they were new.
What, mute Balurdo?

speeches.speaker: Feli.
prose:
I in faith, & twere not for printing, and painting,
my breech, and your face would be out of reparation.

speeches.speaker: Bal.
prose:
I, an faith, and twere not for printing, & pointing,
my breech, and your face would be out of reparation.

speeches.speaker: Fel.
prose: Good againe, Echo.

speeches.speaker: Fla.
prose: Thou art, by nature, too foule to be affected.

speeches.speaker: Feli.
verse: And thou, by Art, too faire to be beloued.
By wits life, most sparke spirits, but hard chance.
La ty dine.

speeches.speaker: Pie.
verse: Gallants, the night growes old; & downy sleep
Courts vs, to entertaine his company:
Our tyred lymbes, brus'd in the morning fight,
Intreat soft rest, and gentle husht repose.
Fill out Greeke wines; prepare fresh cressit-light:
Weele haue a banquet: Princes, then good night.

speeches.speaker: An.
verse: What meanes these scattred looks? why tremble you?
Why quake your thoughts, in your distracted eyes?
Collect your spirits, Madam; what doe you see?
Dost not beholde a ghost?
Look, look where he stalks, wrapt vp in clouds of grief,
Darting his sowle, vpon thy wondring eyes.
Looke, he comes towards thee; see, he stretcheth out
His wretched armes to girt thy loued waste,
With a most wisht embrace: see'st him not yet?
Nor yet? Ha, Mellida; thou well maist erre:
For looke; he walkes not like Antonio:
Like that Antonio, that this morning shone,
In glistering habilliments of armes,
To seize his loue, spight of her fathers spite:
But like himselfe, wretched, and miserable,
Banisht, forlorne, despairing, strook quite through,
With sinking griefe, rowld vp in seauen-fould doubles
Of plagues, vanquishable: harke, he speakes to thee.

speeches.speaker: Mell.
verse: Alas, I can not heare, nor see him.

speeches.speaker: Anto.
verse: Why? al this night about the roome he stalkt,
And groand, and houl'd, with raging passion,
To view his loue (life blood of all his hopes,
Crowne of his fortunes) clipt by strangers armes.
Looke but behinde thee.

speeches.speaker: Mel.
verse: O, Antonio; my Lord, my Loue, my

speeches.speaker: An.
verse: Leaue passion, sweet; for time, place, aire, & earth,
Are all our foes: feare, and be iealous; faire,
Lets fly.

speeches.speaker: Mell.
verse: Deare heart; ha, whether?

speeches.speaker: Anto.
verse: O, tis no matter whether, but lets fly.
Ha! now I thinke ont, I haue nere a home:
No father, friend, no country to imbrace
These wretched limbes: the world, the All that is,
Is all my foe: a prince not worth a doite:
Onelie my head is hoised to high rate,
Worth twentie thousand double Pistolets,
To him that can but strike it from these shoulders.
But come sweete creature, thou shalt be my home;
My father, country, riches, and my friend:
My all, my soule; and thou and I will liue:
(Lets thinke like what) and thou and I will liue
Like vnmatcht mirrors of calamitie.
The iealous eare of night eaue-drops our talke.
Holde thee, thers a iewell; & look thee, thers a note
That will direct thee when, where, how to fly;
Bid me adieu.

speeches.speaker: Mell.
verse: Farewell bleak misery.

speeches.speaker: Anto.
verse: Stay sweet, lets kisse before you goe.

speeches.speaker: Mel.
verse: Farewell deare soule.

speeches.speaker: Anto.
verse: Farewell my life, my heart.

speeches.speaker: Andr.
verse: IS not yon gleame, the shuddering morne that flakes,
With siluer tinctur, the east vierge of heauen?

speeches.speaker: Lu.
verse: I thinke it is, so please your excellence.

speeches.speaker: Andr.
verse: Away, I haue no excellence to please.
Pree the obserue the custome of the world,
That onely flatters greatnesse, States exalts.
And please my excellence! O Lucio.
Thou hast bin euer held respected deare,
Euen pretious to Andrugios in most loue.
Good, flatter not. Nay, if thou giu'st not faith
That I am wretched, O read that, read that.
prose:
Piero Sforza, to the Italian
Princes, fortune.
EXCELLENT, the iust ouerthrowe, Andrugio
tooke in the Venetian gulfe, hath so assured the Genowaies
of the iustice of his cause, and the hatefulnesse of his
person, that they haue banisht him and all his family: and,
for confirmation of their peace with vs, haue vowed, that if
he, or his sonne, can be attached, to send vs both their heads.
Wee therefore, by force of our vnited league, forbid you to
harbour him, or his blood: but if you apprehend his person,
we intreat you to send him, or his head, to vs. For wee vowe
by the honour of our blood, to recompence any man that
bringeth his head, with twentie thousand double Pistolets,
and the indeering to our choysest loue.


From Venice: PIERO SFORZA.

speeches.speaker: Andr.
verse: My thoughts are fixt in contemplation
Why this huge earth, this monstrous animal,
That eates her children, should not haue eyes & ears.
Philosophie maintaines that Natur's wise,
And formes no vselesse or vnperfect thing.
Did Nature make the earth, or the earth Nature?
For earthly durt makes all things, makes the man,
Moulds me vp honour; and like a cunning Dutchma~,
Paints me a puppit euen with seeming breath,
And giues a sot appearance of a soule,
Goe to, goe to; thou liest Philosophy.
Nature formes things vnperfect, vselesse, vaine.
Why made she not the earth with eyes and eares?
That she might see desert, and heare mens plaints:
That when a soule is splitted, sunke with griefe,
He might fall thus, vpon the breast of earth;
And in her eare, halloo his misery:
Exclaming thus. O thou all bearing earth,
Which men doe gape for, till thou cramst their mouths,
And choakst their throts with dust: O chaune thy brest,
And let me sinke into thee. Looke who knocks;
Andrugio cals. But O, she's deafe and blinde.
A wretch, but leane reliefe on earth can finde.

speeches.speaker: Lu.
verse: Sweet Lord, abandon passion, and disarme.
Since by the fortune of the tumbling sea,
We are rowl'd vp, vpon the Venice marsh,
Lets clip all fortune, least more lowring fate

speeches.speaker: And.
verse: More lowring fate? O Lucio, choak that breath.
Now I defie chaunce. Fortunes browe hath frown'd,
Euen to the vtmost wrinkle it can bend:
Her venom's spit. Alas, what country rests,
What sonne, what comfort that she can depriue?
Tryumphes not Venice in my ouerthrow?
Gapes not my natiue country for my blood?
Lies not my sonne tomb'd in the swelling maine?
And yet more lowring fate? There's nothing left
Vnto Andrugio, but Andrugio:
And that nor mischief, force, distresse, nor hel can take.
Fortune my fortunes, not my minde shall shake.

speeches.speaker: Lu.
verse: Speake like your selfe: but giue me leaue, my Lord,
To wish your safetie. If you are but seene,
Your armes display you; therefore put them off,
And take

speeches.speaker: And.
verse: Would'st thou haue me go vnarm'd among my foes?
Being besieg'd by passion, entring lists,
To combat with despaire and mightie griefe:
My soule beleaguerd with the crushing strength
Of sharpe impatience. Ha Lucio, goe vnarm'd?
Come soule, resume the valour of thy brith;
My selfe, my selfe will dare all opposits:
Ile muster forces, an vnuanquisht power:
Cornets of horse shall presse th'vngratefull earth;
This hollow wombed masse shall inly grone,
And murmur to sustaine the waight of armes:
Gastly amazement, with vpstarted haire,
Shall hurry on before, and vsher vs,
Whil'st trumpets clamour, with a sound of death.

speeches.speaker: Lu.
verse: Peace, good my Lord, your speach is al too light.
Alas, suruey your fortunes, looke what's left
Of all your forces, and your vtmost hopes?
A weake old man, a Page, and your poore selfe.

speeches.speaker: And.
verse: Andrugio liues, and a faire cause of armes,
Why that's an armie all inuincible.
He who hath that, hath a battalion
Royal, armour of proofe, huge troups of barbed steeds,
Maine squares of pikes, millions of harguebush.
O, a faire cause stands firme, and will abide.
Legions of Angels fight vpon her side.

speeches.speaker: Lu.
verse: Then, noble spirit, slide in strange disguise,
Vnto some gratious Prince, and soiourne there,
Till time, and fortune giue reuenge firme meanes.

speeches.speaker: And.
verse: No, ile not trust the honour of a man:
Golde is growne great, and makes perfidiousnesse
A common water in most Princes Courts:
He's in the Chekle-roule: Ile not trust my blood;
I know none breathing, but will cogge a dye
For twentie thousand double Pistolets.
How goes the time?

speeches.speaker: Luc.
prose: I saw no sunne to day.

speeches.speaker: And.
verse: No sun wil shine, where poor Andrugio breaths,
My soule growes heauie: boy let's haue a song:
Weele sing yet, faith, euen despite of fate.

speeches.speaker: And.
verse: Tis a good boy, & by my troth, well sung.
O, and thou felt'st my griefe, I warrant thee,
Thou would'st haue strook diuision to the height;
And made the life of musicke breath: hold boy: why so?
For Gods sake call me not Andrugio,
That I may soone forget what I haue bin.
For heauens name, name not Antonio;
That I may not remember he was mine.
Well, ere yon sunne set, ile shew my selfe my selfe,
Worthy my blood. I was a Duke; that's all.
No matter whether, but from whence we fall.

speeches.speaker: Fe.
verse: Castilio? Alberto? Balurdo? none vp?
Forobosco? Flattery, nor thou vp yet:
Then there's no Courtier stirring: that's firme truth?
I cannot sleepe: Feliche seldome rests
In these court lodgings. I haue walkt all night,
To see if the nocturnall court delights
Could force me enuie their felicitie:
And by plaine troth; I will confesse plaine troth:
I enuie nothing, but the Trauense light.
O, had it eyes, and eares, and tongues, it might
See sport, heare speach of most strange surquedries.
O, if that candle-light were made a Poet,
He would prooue a rare firking Satyrist,
And drawe the core forth of impostum'd sin.
Well, I thanke heauen yet, that my content
Can enuie nothing, but poore candle-light.
As for the other glistering copper spangs,
That glisten in the tyer of the Court,
Praise God, I eyther hate, or pittie them.
Well here ile sleepe till that the sceane of vp
Is past at Court. O calme husht rich content,
Is there a being blessednesse without thee?
How soft thou down'st the couch where thou dost rest,
Nectar to life, thou sweet Ambrosian feast.

speeches.speaker: Cast.
verse: Am not I a most sweete youth now?

speeches.speaker: Cat.
verse: Yes, when your throat's perfum'd; your verie words
Doe smell of Amber greece. O stay sir, stay;
Sprinkle some sweete water to your shooes heeles,
That your mistresse may swear you haue a sweet foot.

speeches.speaker: Cast.
verse: Good, very good, very passing passing good.

speeches.speaker: Fel.
prose:
Fut, what trebble minikin squeaks there, ha? good?
very good, very very good?

speeches.speaker: Casti.
verse: I will warble to the delicious concaue of my
Mistresse eare: and strike her thoughts with
The pleasing touch of my voice.

speeches.speaker: Cast.
verse: Feliche, health, fortune, mirth, and wine,

speeches.speaker: Fel.
verse: To thee my loue diuine.

speeches.speaker: Cast.
verse: I drinke to thee, sweeting.

speeches.speaker: Fel.
verse: Plague on thee for an Asse.

speeches.speaker: Cast.
prose:
Now thou hast seene the Court; by the perfecction
of it, dost not enuie it?

speeches.speaker: Fel.
verse: I wonder it doth not enuie me.
Why man, I haue bene borne vpon the spirits wings,
The soules swift Pegasus, the fantasie:
And from the height of contemplation,
Haue view'd the feeble ioynts men totter on.
I enuie none; but hate, or pittie all.
For when I viewe, with an intentiue thought,
That creature faire; but proud; him rich, but sot:
Th'other wittie; but vnmeasured arrogant:
Him great; yet boundlesse in ambition:
Him high borne; but of base life: to' ther feard;
Yet feared feares, and fears most, to be most loued:
Him wise; but made a foole for publick vse:
Th'other learned, but selfe-opinionate:
When I discourse all these, and see my selfe
Nor faire, nor rich, nor wittie, great, nor fear'd:
Yet amply suted, with all full content:
Lord, how I clap my hands, and smooth my brow,
Rubbing my quiet bosome, tossing vp
A gratefull spirit to omnipotence!

speeches.speaker: Cast.
verse: Ha, ha: but if thou knew'st my happinesse,
Thou wouldst euen grate away thy soule to dust,
In enuy of my sweete beatitude:
I can not sleepe for kisses; I can not rest
For Ladies letters, that importune me
With such vnused vehemence of loue,
Straight to solicit them, that

speeches.speaker: Feli.
verse: Confusion seize me, but I thinke thou lyest.
Why should I not be sought to then aswell?
Fut, me thinks, I am as like a man.
Troth, I haue a good head of haire, a cheeke
Not as yet wan'd; a legge, faith, in the full.
I ha not a red beard, take not tobacco much:
And S'lid, for other parts of manlinesse

speeches.speaker: Cast.
verse:
Pew waw, you nere accourted them in
pompe:
Put your good parts in presence, gratiously.
Ha, and you had, why they would ha come of, sprung
To your armes: and su'd, and prai'd, and vow'd;
And opened all their sweetnesse to your loue.

speeches.speaker: Fel.
verse: There are a number of such things, as then
Haue often vrg'd me to such loose beliefe:
But S'lid you all doe lye, you all doe lie.
I haue put on good cloathes, and smugd my face,
Strook a faire wench, with a smart speaking eye:
Courted in all sorts, blunt, and passionate;
Had opportunitie put them to the ah:
And, by this light, I finde them wondrous chaste,
Impregnable; perchance a kisse, or so:
But for the rest, O most inexorable.

speeches.speaker: Cast.
verse: Nay then ifaith, pree thee looke here.

speeches.speaker: Fel.
verse: To her most esteemed, lou'd, and generous seruant, Sig.
Castilio Balthazar.
Pree the from whome comes this? faith I must see.
Nay, god's my comfort, I must see the rest;
I must, sans ceremonie, faith I must.

speeches.speaker: Cast.
prose:
O, you spoyle my ruffe, vnset my haire; good
away.

speeches.speaker: Fel.
prose:
Item for strait canuas, thirteene pence, halfe
penny. Item for an elle and a halfe of taffata to couer
your olde canuas dubblet, foureteen shillings, & three
pence. S'light, this a tailors bill.

speeches.speaker: Cast.
verse: In sooth it is the outside of her letter; on which
I tooke the copie of a tailors bill.

speeches.speaker: Dil.
prose:
But tis not crost, I am sure of that. Lord haue
mercie on him, his credit hath giuen vp the last gaspe.
Faith ile leaue him; for hee lookes as melancholy as
a wench the first night she

speeches.speaker: Feli.
Cast.
prose:
And tell not my Ladie mother. Well, as I am
true gentleman, if she had not wild me on her blessing,
not to spoyle my face; if I could not finde in my heart
to fight, would I might nere eate a Potatoe pye more.

speeches.speaker: Fel.
prose:
More foole, more rare fooles! O, for time and
place, long enough, and large enough, to acte these
fooles! Here might be made a rare Scene of folly, if
the plat could beare it.

speeches.speaker: Bal.
prose:
By the suger-candy sky, holde vp the glasse
higher, that I may see to sweare in fashion. O, one loofe
more would ha made them shine; gods neakes, they
would haue shone like my mystresse browe. Euen so
the Duke frownes for all this Cursond world: oh that
gerne kils, it kils. By my golden What's the richest
thing about me?

speeches.speaker: Dil.
prose: Your teeth.

speeches.speaker: Bal.
prose:
By my golden teeth, hold vp; that I may put in:
hold vp, I say, that I may see to put on my gloues.

speeches.speaker: Dil.
prose:
O, delicious sweet cheekt master, if you discharge
but one glance from the leuell of that set face: O, you
will strike a wench; youle make any wench loue you.

speeches.speaker: Balur.
prose:
By Iesu, I think I am as elegant a Courtier,
as How lik'st thou my suite?

speeches.speaker: Catz.
prose:
All, beyond all, no peregal: you are wondred at,
for an asse.

speeches.speaker: Bal.
prose:
Well, Dildo, no christen creature shall knowe
hereafter, what I will doe for thee heretofore.

speeches.speaker: Ros.
prose: Here wants a little white, Flauia.

speeches.speaker: Dil.
prose:
I, but master, you haue one little falt; you sleepe
open mouth'd.

speeches.speaker: Ball.
prose:
Pewe, thou iestst. In good sadnesse, Ile haue a
looking glasse nail'd to the the testarn of the bed, that
I may see when I sleep, whether tis so, or not; take heed
you lye not: goe to, take heede you lie not.

speeches.speaker: Fla.
prose:
By my troth, you looke as like the princesse, now
I, but her lip is lip is a little redder, a very little
redder: but by the helpe of Art, or Nature, ere I cha~ge
my perewigge, mine shall be as red.

speeches.speaker: Fla.
prose:
O, I, that face, that eye, that smile, that writhing of
your bodie, that wanton dandling of your fan, becoms
prethely, so sweethly, tis euen the goodest Ladie that
breathes, the most amiable Faith the fringe of
your sattin peticote is ript. Good faith madam, they say
you are the most bounteous Lady to your women, that
euer O most delitious beautie! Good Madam
let me kith it.

speeches.speaker: Feli.
prose:
Rare sport, rare sport! A female foole, and a female
flatterer.

speeches.speaker: Ross.
prose: Bodie a mee, the Duke: away the glasse.

speeches.speaker: Pie.
prose: Take vp your paper, Rossaline.

speeches.speaker: Rossa.
prose: Not mine, my Lord.

speeches.speaker: Pie.
prose: Not yours, my Ladie? Ile see what tis.

speeches.speaker: Bal.
prose:
And how does my sweete mistresse? O Ladie
deare, euen as tis an olde say, Tis an old horse can neither
wighy, nor wagge his taile: euen so doe I holde
my set face still: euen so, tis a bad courtier that can neither
discourse, nor blow his nose.

speeches.speaker: Pie.
verse: O trista traditriche, rea, ribalda fortuna,
Negando mi vindetta mi causa fera morte,
prose:
Meet me at Abrahams, the Iewes, where I bought
my Amazons disguise. A shippe lies in the port, ready
bound for England; make haste, come priuate.

Antonio, Forobosco, Alberto, Feliche, Castilio, Balurdo? run,
keepe the Palace, post to the ports, goe to my daughters
chamber: whether now? scud to the Iewes, stay,
runne to the gates, stop the gundolets, let none passe
the marsh, doe all at once. Antonio? his head, his head.
Keep you the Court, the rest stand still, or runne, or
goe, or shoute, or search, or scud, or call, or hang, or
doe doe doe, su su su, somthing: I know not who who
who, what I do do do, nor who who who, where
I am.

speeches.speaker: Fel.
prose: Ha ha ha. I could breake my splene at his impatience.

speeches.speaker: Anto.
verse: Alma & gratiosa fortuna sia^e fauor evole,
Et fortunati siano vnoti del mia dulce Mellida, Mellida.

speeches.speaker: Mel.
verse: Alas Antonio, I haue lost thy note.
A number mount my staires; ile straight returne.

speeches.speaker: Fel.
verse: Antonio,
Be not affright, sweete Prince; appease thy feare,
Buckle thy spirits vp, put all thy wits
In wimble action, or thou art surpriz'd.

speeches.speaker: Anto.
verse: I care not.

speeches.speaker: Fel.
verse: Art mad, or desperate? or

speeches.speaker: Anto.
verse: Both, both, all, all: I pree thee let mee ly;
Spight of you all, I can, and I will dy.

speeches.speaker: Fel.
verse: You are distraught; O, this is madnesse breath.

speeches.speaker: An.
verse: Each man take hence life, but no man death:
Hee's a good fellow, and keepes open house:
A thousand thousand waies lead to his gate,
To his wide mouth'd porch: when niggard life
Hath but one little, little wicket through.
We wring our selues into this wretched world,
To pule, and weepe, exclaime, to curse and raile,
To fret, and ban the fates, to strike the earth
As I doe now. Antonio, curse thy birth,
And die.

speeches.speaker: Fel.
verse: Nay, heauens my comfort, now you are peruerse;
You know I alwaies lou'd you; pree thee liue.

Wilt thou strike deade thy friends, drawe mourning
teares

speeches.speaker: An.
verse: Alas, Feliche, I ha nere a friend;
No country, father, brother, kinsman left
To weepe my fate, or sigh my funerall:
I roule but vp and downe, and fill a seat
In the darke caue of dusky misery.

speeches.speaker: Feli.
verse: Fore heauen, the Duke comes: hold you, take my key,
Slinke to my chamber, looke you; that is it:
There shall you finde a suite I wore at sea:
Take it, and slippe away. Nay, pretious,
If youle be peeuish, by this light, Ile sweare,
Thou rail'dst vpon thy loue before thou dyedst,
And call'd her strumpet.

speeches.speaker: Ant.
verse: Sheele not credit thee.

speeches.speaker: Fel.
verse: Tut, that's all one: ile defame thy loue;
And make thy deade trunke held in vile regard.

speeches.speaker: Ant.
verse: Wilt needs haue it so? why then Antonio,
Viue esperanza, in despetto dell fato.

speeches.speaker: Piero.
verse: O, my sweet Princes, was't not brauely found?
Euen there I found the note, euen there it lay.
I kisse the place for ioy, that there it lay.
This way he went, here let vs make a stand:
Ile keepe this gate my selfe: O gallant youth!
Ile drinke carouse vnto your countries health,
Euen in Antonio's scull.

speeches.speaker: Bal.
prose:
Lord blesse vs: his breath is more fearefull then
a Sergeants voice, when he cries; I arrest.

speeches.speaker: Ant.
verse: Stoppe Antonio, keepe, keepe Antonio.

speeches.speaker: Piero.
verse: Where, where man, where?

speeches.speaker: Ant.
verse:
Here, here: let me me pursue him downe the
marsh.

speeches.speaker: Pie.
verse: Hold, there's my signet, take a gundelet:
Bring me his head, his head, and by mine honour,
Ile make thee the wealthiest Mariner that breathes.

speeches.speaker: Anto.
verse: Ile sweate my bloode out, till I haue him safe.

speeches.speaker: Pie.
verse: Speake heartily ifaith, good Mariner.
O, wee will mount in tryumph: soone, at night,
Ile set his head vp. Lets thinke where.

speeches.speaker: Bal.
prose:
Vp on his shoulders, that's the fittest place for
it. If it be not as fit as if it were made for them; say, Balurdo,
thou art a sot, an asse.

speeches.speaker: Pie.
verse: Sprightly, ifaith. In troth he's somwhat like
My daughter Mellida: but alas poore soule,
Her honour heeles, god knowes, are halfe so light.

speeches.speaker: Mel.
verse: Escap't I am, spite of my fathers spight.

speeches.speaker: Pie.
verse: Ho, this will warme my bosome ere I sleepe.

speeches.speaker: Fla.
verse: O my Lord, your daughter.

speeches.speaker: Pie.
verse: I, I, my daughter's safe enough, I warrant thee.
This vengeance on the boy will lengthen out
My daies vnmeasuredly.
It shall be chronicled, time to come;
Piero Sforza slewe Andrugio's sonne.

speeches.speaker: Fla.
verse: I, but my Lord, your daughter.

speeches.speaker: Pie.
verse: I, I, my good wench, she is safe enough.

speeches.speaker: Fla.
verse: O, then, my Lord, you know she's run away.

speeches.speaker: Pie.
verse: Run away, away, how run away?

speeches.speaker: Fla.
verse: She's vanisht in an instante, none knowes whether.

speeches.speaker: Pie.
verse: Pursue, pursue, fly, run, post, scud away.
Fly, call, run, rowe, ride, cry, shout, hurry, haste:
Haste, hurry, shoute, cry, ride, rowe, run, call, fly
Backward and forward, euery way about.
Maldetta fortuna ^hy condura sorta
Che faro, che diro, pur fugir tanto mal!

speeches.speaker: Cast.
verse: Twas you that struck me euen now: was it not?

speeches.speaker: Fel.
verse: It was I that struck you euen now.

speeches.speaker: Cast.
verse: You bastinadoed me, I take it.

speeches.speaker: Fel.
verse: I bastinadoed you, and you tooke it.

speeches.speaker: Cast.
prose:
Faith sir, I haue the richest Tobacco in the court
for you; I would be glad to make you satisfaction, if I
haue wronged you. I would not the Sun should set vpon
your anger; giue me your hand.

speeches.speaker: Fel.
prose:
Content faith, so thou'lt breede no more such lies.
I hate not man, but mans lewd qualities.

speeches.speaker: Ant.
verse: STOP, stop Antonio, stay Antonio.
Vaine breath, vaine breath, Antonio's lost;
He can not finde himselfe, not seize himselfe.
Alas, this that you see, is not Antonio,
His spirit houers in Piero's Court,
Hurling about his agill faculties,
To apprehend the sight of Mellida:
But poore, poore soule, wanting apt instruments
To speake or see, stands dumbe and blinde, sad spirit,
Roul'd vp in gloomie clouds as black as ayer,
Through which the rustie coach of Night is drawne:
Tis so, ile giue you instance that tis so.
Conceipt you me. As hauing clasp't a rose
Within my palme, the rose being tane away,
My hand retaines a little breath of sweete:
So may mans trunke; his spirit slipt awaie,
Holds still a faint perfume of his sweet ghest.
Tis so; for when discursiue powers fl^e out,
And rome in progresse, through the bou~ds of heauen,
The soule it selfe gallops along with them,
As chiefetaine of this winged troope of thought,
Whilst the dull lodge of spirit standeth waste,
Vntill the soule returne from What wast I said?
O, this is naught, but speckling melancholie.
I haue beene
That Morpheus tender skinp Cosen germane
Beare with me good
Mellida: clod vpon clod thus fall.
Hell is beneath; yet heauen is ouer all.

speeches.speaker: And.
verse: Come Lucio, lets goe eat: what hast thou got?
Rootes, rootes? alas, they are seeded, new cut vp.
O, thou hast wronged Nature, Lucio:
But bootes not much; thou but pursu'st the world,
That cuts off vertue, fore it comes to growth,
Least it should seed, and so orerun her sonne,
Dull pore-blinde error. Giue me water, boy.
There is no poison in't I hope, they say
That lukes in massie plate: and yet the earth
Is so infected with a generall plague,
That hee's most wise, that thinks there's no man foole:
Right prudent, that esteemes no creature iust:
Great policy the least things to mistrust.
Giue me Assay How we mock greatnesse now!

speeches.speaker: Lu.
verse: A strong conceipt is rich, so most men deeme:
If not to be, tis comfort yet to seeme.

speeches.speaker: And.
verse: Why man, I neuer was a Prince till now.
Tis not the bared pate, the bended knees,
Guilt tipstaues, Tyrrian purple, chaires of state,
Troopes of pide butterflies, that flutter still
In greatnesse summer, that confirme a prince:
Tis not the vnsauory breath of multitudes,
Showting and clapping, with confused dinne;
That makes a Prince. No Lucio, he's a king,
A true right king, that dares doe aught, saue wrong,
Feares nothing mortall, but to be vniust,
Who is not blowne vp with the flattering puffes
Of spungy Sycophants: Who stands vnmou'd,
Despight the iustling of opinion:
Who can enioy himselfe, maugre the throng
That striue to presse his quiet out of him:
Who sits vpon Ioues footestoole, as I doe,
Adoring, not affecting, maiestie:
Whose brow is wreathed with the siluer crowne
Of cleare content: this, Lucio, is a king.
And of this empire, euery man's possest,
That's worth his soule.

speeches.speaker: Lu.
verse: My Lord, the Genowaies had wont to say

speeches.speaker: And.
verse: Name not the Genowaies: that very word
Vnkings me quite, makes me vile passions slaue.
O, you that made open the glibbery Ice
Of vulgar fauour, viewe Andrugio.
Was neuer Prince with more applause confirm'd,
With louder shouts of tryumph launched out
Into the surgy maine of gouernment:
Was neuer Prince with more despight cast out,
Left shipwrackt, banisht, on more guiltlesse ground.
O rotten props of the craz'd multitude,
How you stil double, faulter, vnder the lightest chance
That straines your vaines. Alas, one battle lost,

Your whorish loue, your drunken healths, your houts
and shouts,
Your smooth God saue's, and all your diuels last
That tempts our quiet, to your hell of throngs.
Spit on me Lucio, for I am turnd slaue:
Obserue how passion domineres ore me.

speeches.speaker: Lu.
verse: No wonder, noble Lord, hauing lost a sonne,
A country, crowne, and

speeches.speaker: And.
verse: I Lucio, hauing lost a sonne, a sonne,
A country, house, crowne, sonne. O lares, misereri lares.
Which shall I first deplore? My sonne, my sonne,
My deare sweete boy, my deare Antonio.

speeches.speaker: Ant.
verse: Antonio?

speeches.speaker: And.
verse: I, eccho, I; I meane Antonio.

speeches.speaker: Ant.
verse: Antonio, who meanes Antonio?

speeches.speaker: Ant.
verse: Where art? what art? know'st thou Antonio?

speeches.speaker: Ant.
verse: Yes.

speeches.speaker: And.
verse: Liues hee?

speeches.speaker: Ant.
verse: No.

speeches.speaker: And.
verse: Where lies hee deade?

speeches.speaker: Ant.
verse: Here.

speeches.speaker: And.
verse: Where?

speeches.speaker: Ant.
verse: Here.

speeches.speaker: Andr.
verse: Art thou Antonio?

speeches.speaker: Ant.
verse: I thinke I am.

speeches.speaker: And.
verse: Dost thou but think? What, dost not know thy selfe?

speeches.speaker: Ant.
verse: He is a foole that thinks he knowes himselfe.

speeches.speaker: And.
verse: Vpon thy faith to heauen, giue thy name.

speeches.speaker: Ant.
verse: I were not worthy of Andrugio's blood,
If I denied my name's Antonio.

speeches.speaker: And.
verse: I were not worthy to be call'd thy father,
If I denied my name Andrugio.
And dost thou liue? O, let me kisse thy cheeke,
And deaw thy browe with trickling drops of ioy.
Now heauens will be done: for I haue liu'd
To see my ioy, my sonne Antonio.
Giue my thy hand; now fortune doe thy worst,
His blood, that lapt thy spirit in the wombe,
Thus (in his loue) will make his armes thy tombe.

speeches.speaker: Ant.
verse: Blesse not the bodie with your twining armes,
Which is accurst of heauen. O, what black sinne
Hath bin committed by our auntient house,
Whose scalding vengeance lights vpon our heads,
That thus the world, and fortune casts vs out,
As loathed obiects, ruines branded slaues.

speeches.speaker: And.
verse: Doe not expostulate the heauens will:
But, O, remember to forget thy selfe:
Forget remembrance what thou once hast bin.
Come, creepe with me from out this open ayre.
Euen trees haue tongues, and will betray our life.
I am a raising of our house, my boy:
Which fortune will not enuie, tis so meane,
And like the world (all durt) there shalt thou rippe
The inwards of thy fortunes, in mine eares,
Whilst I sit weeping, blinde with passions teares:
Then ile begin, and weele such order keepe,
That one shall still tell greefes, the other weepe.

speeches.speaker: Ant.
verse: Ile follow you. Boy, pree thee stay a little.
Thou hast had a good voice, if this colde marshe,
Wherein we lurke, haue not corrupted it.
I pree thee sing, but sirra (marke you me)
Let each nore breath the heart of passion,
The sad extracture of extreamest griefe.
Make me a straine; speake, groning like a bell,
That towles departing soules.
Breath me a point that may inforce me weepe,
To wring my hands, to breake my cursed breast,
Raue, and exclaime, lie groueling on the earth,
Straight start vp frantick, crying, Mellida.
Sing but, Antonio hath lost Mellida,
And thou shalt see mee (like a man possest)
Howle out such passion, that euen this brinish marsh
Will squease out teares, from out his spungy cheekes,
The rocks euen groane, and
Pree thee, pree thee sing:
Or I shall nere ha done when I am in.
Tis harder for me end, then to begin.
For looke thee boy, my griefe that hath no end,
I may begin to playne, but pree thee sing.

speeches.speaker: Mell.
verse: Heauen keepe you sir.

speeches.speaker: An.
verse: Heauen keepe you from me, sir.

speeches.speaker: Mell.
verse: I must be acquainted with you, sir.

speeches.speaker: Ant.
verse: Wherefore? Art thou infected with misery,
Sear'd with the anguish of calamitie?
Art thou true sorrow, hearty griefe, canst weepe?
I am not for thee if thou canst not raue,
Fall flat on the ground, and thus exclaime on heauen;
O trifling Nature, why enspiredst thou breath

speeches.speaker: Mell.
verse: Stay sir, I thinke you named Mellida.

speeches.speaker: Ant.
verse: Know'st thou Mellida?

speeches.speaker: Mel.
verse: Yes.

speeches.speaker: Ant.
verse: Hast thou seene Mellida?

speeches.speaker: Mell.
verse: Yes.

speeches.speaker: Ant.
verse: Then hast thou seene the glory of her sex,
The musick of Nature, the vnequall'd lustre
Of vnmatched excellence, the vnited sweete
Of heauens graces, the most adored beautie,
That euer strooke amazement in the world.

speeches.speaker: Mell.
verse: You seeme to loue her.

speeches.speaker: Ant.
verse: With my very soule.

speeches.speaker: Mell.
verse: Shele not requite it: all her loue is fixt
Vpon a gallant, on Antonio,
The Duke of Genoas sonne. I was her Page:
And often as I waited, she would sigh;
O, deere Antonio; and to strengthen thought,
Would clip my neck, and kisse, and kisse me thus.
Therefore leaue louing her: fa, faith me thinks,
Her beautie is not halfe so rauishing
As you discourse of; she hath a freckled face,
A lowe forehead, and a lumpish eye.

speeches.speaker: Ant.
verse: O heauen, that I should heare such blasphemie.
Boy, rogue, thou liest, and
Spauento dell mio core dolce Mellida,
Di graua morte restor^ vero dolce Mellida,
Celesta saluatrice sovrana Mellida
Del mio sperar; trofeo vero Mellida.

speeches.speaker: Mel.
verse: Diletta & soaue anima mia Antonio,
Godeuole belezza cortese Antonio.
Signior mio & virginal amore bell' Antonio
Gusto delli mei sensi, car' Antonio.

speeches.speaker: Ant.
verse: O suamisce il cor in vn soaue baccio,

speeches.speaker: Mel.
verse: Murono i sensi nel desiato dessio:

speeches.speaker: Ant.
verse: Nel Cielo puo lesser belta pia chiara.

speeches.speaker: Mel.
verse: Nel mondo pol esser belta pia chiara?

speeches.speaker: Ant.
verse: Dammi vn baccio da quella bocca beata,
Bassiammi, coglier l' aur a odorata
Che in sua neggia in quello dolce labra.

speeches.speaker: Mel.
verse: Dammi pimpero del tuo gradit' amore
Che beame, cosempiterno honore,
Cosi, cosimi conuerra morir.
Good sweet, scout ore the marsh: for my heart trembls
At euery little breath that strikes my eare,
When thou returnest: and ile discourse
How I deceiu'd the Court: then thou shall tell
How thou escapt'st the watch: weele point our speech
With amorous kissing, kissing co~maes, and euen suck
The liquid breath from out each others lips.

speeches.speaker: Ant.
verse: Dul clod, no man but such sweeet fauour clips.
I goe, and yet my panting blood perswades me stay.
Turne coward in her sight? away, away.
prose:
I thinke confusion of Babell is falne vpon these louers,
that they change their language, but I feare mee, my
master hauing but fained the person of a woman, hath
got their vnfained imperfection, and is growne double
tongu'd: as for Mellida, she were no woman, if shee
could not yeelde strange language. But howsoeuer, if I
should sit in iudgement, tis an errour easier to be pardoned
by the auditors, then excused by the authours;
and yet some priuate respect may rebate the edge of
the keener censure.

speeches.speaker: Pie.
prose:
This way shee took: search, my sweet gentleme~.
How now Balurdo, canst thou meete with any body?

speeches.speaker: Bal.
prose:
As I am true gentleman, I made my horse sweat,
that he hath nere a dry thread on him: and I can meete
with no liuing creature, but men & beastes, In good
sadnesse, I would haue sworne I had seene Mellida euen
now: for I sawe a thing stirre vnder a hedge, and I
peep't, and I spyed a thing: and I peer'd, and I tweerd
vnderneath: and truly a right wise man might haue
beene deceiued: for it was

speeches.speaker: Pie.
verse: What, in the name of heauen?

speeches.speaker: Bal.
verse: A dun cowe.

speeches.speaker: Fel.
verse: Sh'ad nere a kettle on her head?

speeches.speaker: Pie.
verse: Boy, didst thou see a yong Lady passe this way?

speeches.speaker: Gal.
verse: Why speake you not?

speeches.speaker: Bal.
prose:
Gods neakes, proud elfe, giue the Duke rouerence,
stand bare with a
Whogh! heauens blesse me: Mellida, Mellida.

speeches.speaker: Pie.
verse: Where man, where?

speeches.speaker: Balur.
prose:
Turnd man, turnd man: women weare the
breaches, loe here,

speeches.speaker: Pie.
verse: Light and vnduteous! kneele not, peeuish elfe,
Speake not, entreate not, shame vnto my house,
Curse to my honour. Where's Antonio?
Thou traitresse to my hate, what is he shipt
For England now? well whimpering harlot, hence.

speeches.speaker: Mell.
verse: Good father

speeches.speaker: Pie.
prose:
Good me no goods. Seest thou that sprightly
youth? ere thou canst tearme to morrow morning old,
thou shalt call him thy husband, Lord and loue.

speeches.speaker: Mel.
verse: Ay me.

speeches.speaker: Pie.
verse: Blirt on your ay mees, gard her safely hence.
Drag her away, ile be your gard to night.
Young Prince, mount vp your spirits, and prepare
To solemnize your Nuptials eue with popme.

speeches.speaker: Gal.
verse: The time is scant: now nimble wits appeare:
Phoebus begins gleame, the welkin's cleare.

speeches.speaker: Bal.
verse: Now nimble wits appeare: ile my selfe appeare,
Balurdo's selfe, that in quick wit doth surpasse,
Will shew the substance of a compleat

speeches.speaker: Dil.
verse: Asse, asse.

speeches.speaker: Bal.
verse: Ile mount my courser, and most gallantly prick

speeches.speaker: Dil.
prose:
Gallantly prick is too long, and stands hardly
in the verse, sir.

speeches.speaker: Bal.
prose:
Ile speake pure rime, and will so brauely pranke
it, that ile tosse loue like a pranke, pranke it: a rime for
pranke it?

speeches.speaker: Dil.
prose: Blankit.

speeches.speaker: Bal.
prose:
That ile tosse loue, like a dogge in a blanket: ha
ha, in deede law. I thinke, ha ha; I thinke ha ha, I think
I shall tickle the Muses. And I strike it not deade, say,
Balurdo, thou art an arrant sot.

speeches.speaker: Dil.
prose: Balurdo, thou art an arrant sot.

speeches.speaker: And.
verse: Now, come vnited force of chap-falne death:
Come, power of fretting anguish, leaue distresse.
O, thus infoulded, we haue breasts of proofe,
Gainst all the venom'd stings of misery.

speeches.speaker: Ant:
verse: Father, now I haue an antidote,
Gainst all the poyson that the world can breath.
My Mellida, my Mellida doth blesse
This bleak waste with her presence. How now boy,
Why dost thou weepe? alas, where's Mellida?

speeches.speaker: Ant.
verse: Ay me, my Lord.

speeches.speaker: And.
verse: A sodden horror doth inuade my blood,
My sinewes tremble, and my panting heart
Scuds round about my bosome so goe out,
Dreading the assailant, horrid passion.
O, be no tyrant, kill me with one blowe.
Speake quickly, briefely boy.

speeches.speaker: Pa.
verse: Her father found, and seis'd her, she is gone.

speeches.speaker: And.
verse: Son, heat thy bloode, be not frose vp with grief.
Courage, sweet boy, sinke not beneath the waight
Of crushing mischiefe. O where's thy dantlesse heart
Thy fathers spirit! I renounce thy blood,
If thou forsake thy valour.

speeches.speaker: Lu.
verse: See how his grief speakes in his flow-pac't steps:
Alas, tis more than he can vtter, let him goe.
Dumbe solitary path best sureth woe.

speeches.speaker: And.
verse: Giue me my armes, my armour Lucio.

speeches.speaker: Lu.
verse: Deare Lord, what means this rage, when lacking vse
Scarce safes your life, will you in armour rise?

speeches.speaker: And.
verse: Fortune feares valour, presseth cowardize.

speeches.speaker: Lu.
verse: Then valour gets applause, when it hath place,
And meanes to blaze it.

speeches.speaker: And.
verse: Nunquam potest non esse.

speeches.speaker: Lu.
verse: Patience, my Lord, may bring your ils some end.

speeches.speaker: And.
verse: What patience, friend, can ruin'd hopes atte~d?
Come, let me die like old Andrugio:
Worthy my birth. O blood-true-honour'd graues
Are farre more blessed then base life of slaues. Exeunt.

speeches.speaker: Bal.
prose:
AND are you a painter sir, can you drawe, can
you drawe?

speeches.speaker: Pay.
prose: Yes sir.

speeches.speaker: Ba.
prose:
Indeede lawe? now so can my fathers forehore
horse. And are these the workmanshippe of your
hands?

speeches.speaker: Payn.
prose: I did lymne them.

speeches.speaker: Bal.
prose:
Lymne them? a good word, lymne them: whose
picture is this? Anno Domini 1599. Beleeue mee,
master Anno Domini was of a good settled age when
you lymn'd him. 1599. yeares old? Lets see the other.
Etatis suae 24. Bir Ladie he is somwhat younger. Belike
master Etatis suae was Anno Dominies sonne.

speeches.speaker: Pa.
prose: Is not your master a

speeches.speaker: Dil.
prose: He hath a little procliuitie to him

speeches.speaker: Pa.
prose:
Procliuitie, good youth? I thank you for your
courtly procliuitie.

speeches.speaker: Bal.
prose:
Approach good sir. I did send for you to drawe
me a deuise, an Imprezza, by Sinecdoche a Mott. By
Phoebus crymson taffata mantle, I thinke I speake as
melodiously, looke you sir, how thinke you ont? I wold
haue you paint mee, for my deuice, a good fat legge of
ewe mutton, swimming in stewde broth of plummes
(boy keele your mouth, it runnes ouer) and the word
shall be; Holde my dish, whilst I spill my pottage. Sure, in
my conscience, twould be the most sweete deuice,
now.

speeches.speaker: Pa.
prose: Twould sent of kitchin-stuffe too much.

speeches.speaker: Bal.
prose:
Gods neakes, now I remember mee, I ha

the rarest deuise in my head that euer breathed. Can
you paint me a driueling reeling song, & let the word
be, Vh.

speeches.speaker: Payn.
prose: A belch.

speeches.speaker: Bal.
prose: O, no no: Vh, paint me vh, or nothing.

speeches.speaker: Pay.
prose:
It can not be done sir, but by a seeming kinde of
drunkennesse.

speeches.speaker: Bal.
prose:
No? well, let me haue a good maff^e ring, with
your owne poesie grauen in it, that must sing a small
trebble, worde for word, thus; And if you will my
true louer be,
Come followe mee to the greene wodde.

speeches.speaker: Pa.
verse: O Lord, sir, I can not make a picture sing.

speeches.speaker: B.
verse: Why? z'lid, I haue seen painted things sing as sweet:
But I hau't will tickle it, for a conceipt ifaith.

speeches.speaker: Alb.
verse: O deare Feliche, giue me thy deuice.
How shall I purchase loue of Rossaline?

speeches.speaker: Fel.
verse: S'will, flatter her soundly.

speeches.speaker: Alb.
verse: Her loue is such, I can not flatter her:
Bu with my vtmost vehemence of speach,
I haue ador'd her beauties.

speeches.speaker: Fel.
prose:
Hast writ good mouing vnaffected rimes to
her.

speeches.speaker: Alb.
verse: O, yes, Feliche, but she scornes my writ.

speeches.speaker: Fel.
verse: Hast thou presented her with sumptuous gifts?

speeches.speaker: Alb.
verse: Alas, my fortunes are too weake to offer them.

speeches.speaker: Fell.
verse: O, then I haue it, Ile tell thee what to doe.

speeches.speaker: Alb.
verse: What, good Feliche?

speeches.speaker: Fel.
verse: Goe and hang thy selfe, I say, goe hang thy selfe,
If that thou canst not giue, goe hang thy selfe:
Ile rime thee dead, or verse thee to the rope.
How thinkst thou of a Poet that sung thus;
Munera sola pacant, sola addunt munera formam:
Munere solicites Pallada, Cypris erit.
Munera, munera.

speeches.speaker: Alb.
verse: Ile goe and breath my woes vnto the rocks,
And spend my griefe vpon the deafest seas.
Ile weepe my passion to the senselesse trees,
And load most solitarie ayre with plaints.
For wods, trees, sea, or rocky Appenine,
Is not so ruthlesse as my Rossaline.
Farewell deare friend, expect no more of mee,
Here ends my part, in this loues Comedy.

speeches.speaker: Fel.
prose: Now master Balurdo, whether are you going, ha?

speeches.speaker: Bal.
prose:
Signior Feliche, how doe you faith, & by my
troth, how doe you?

speeches.speaker: Fel.
verse: Whether art thou going, bully?

speeches.speaker: Bal.
verse: And as heauen helpe mee, how doe you?
How, doe you ifaith he?

speeches.speaker: Fel.
verse: Whether art going man?

speeches.speaker: Bal.
prose:
O god, to the Court, ile be willing to giue you
grace and good countnance, if I may but see you in
the presence.

speeches.speaker: Fel.
prose: O to court? farewell.

speeches.speaker: Bal.
prose:
If you see one in a yellow taffata dubblet, cut
vpon carnation valure, a greene hat, a blewe paire of
veluet hose, a gilt rapier, and an orange ^ny pair of
worsted silke stockings, thats I, thats I.

speeches.speaker: Fel.
prose: Very good, farewell.

speeches.speaker: Bal.
prose:
Ho, you shall knowe me as easily, I ha bought
mee a newe greene feather with a red sprig, you shall
see my wrought shirt hang out at my breeches, you
shall know me.

speeches.speaker: Fel.
prose: Very good, very good, farewell.

speeches.speaker: Ball.
prose:
Marrie in the maske twill be somewhat harde.
But if you heare any bodie speake so wittily, that hee
makes all the roome laugh; that's I, that's I. Farewell
good Signior.

speeches.speaker: Pier.
verse: Aduance the musiques prize, now capring wits,
Rise to your highest mount; let choyce delight
Garland the browe of this tryumphant night.
Sfoote, a sits like Lucifer himselfe.

speeches.speaker: Rossa.
prose:
Good sweete Duke, first let their voyces, strain
for musicks price. Giue mee the golden harpe: faith
with your fauour, ile be vmperesse.

speeches.speaker: Pi.
prose: Sweet neece co~tent: boyes cleare your voice & sing.

speeches.speaker: Rossa.
prose:
By this gould, I had rather haue a seruant with a
short nose, and a thinne haire, then haue such a high
stretcht minikin voice.

speeches.speaker: Pie.
prose: Faire neece, your reason?

speeches.speaker: Ross.
prose:
By the sweete of loue, I should feare extreamely
that he were an Eunuch.

speeches.speaker: Cast.
verse: Sparke spirit, how like you his voice?

speeches.speaker: Ross.
verse: Spark spirit, how like you his voice?
prose:
So helpe me, youth, thy voice squeakes like a dry cork
shoe: come, come; lets heare the next.

speeches.speaker: Pie.
prose:
Trust me, a good strong meane, Well sung my
boy.

speeches.speaker: Bal.
prose:
Hold, hold, hold: are yee blind, could you not see
my voice comming for the harpe. And I knock not diuision
on the head, take hence the harpe, make mee a
slip, and let me goe but for nine pence. Sir Marke, strike
vp for master Balurdo.

verse: Iudgeme~t gentlemen, iudgeme~t. Wast not aboue line?
I appeale to your mouthes that heard my song.
Doe me right, and dub me knight Balurdo.

speeches.speaker: Ros.
prose:
Kneele downe, and ile dub thee knight of the
golden harpe.

speeches.speaker: Ba.
prose: Indeed law, doe, and ile make you Ladie of the siluer fiddlestick,

speeches.speaker: Ross.
prose: Come, kneele, kneele.

speeches.speaker: Bal.
prose: My troth, I thank you, it hath neuer a whistle in't.

speeches.speaker: Ro.
prose:
Naie, good sweet cuz raise vp your drooping eies,

& I were at the point of To haue & to hold, from this
day forward, I would be asham'd to looke thus lumpish.
What my prettie Cuz, tis but the losse of an od
maidenhead: shall's daunce? thou art so sad, harke in
mine eare. I was about to say, but ile forbeare.

speeches.speaker: Ba.
prose:
I come, I come, more then most hunny-suckle
sweete Ladies, pine not for my presence, ile returne
in pompe. Well spoke sir Ieffrey Balurdo. As I am a true
knight, I feele honourable eloquence begin to grope
mee alreadie.

speeches.speaker: Pie.
prose:
Faith, mad neece, I wonder when thou wilt
marrie?

speeches.speaker: Rossa.
prose:
Faith, kinde vncle, when men abandon ielosy,
forsake taking of Tobacco, and cease to weare their
beardes so rudely long. Oh, to haue a husband with
a mouth continually smoaking, with a bush of furs on
the ridge of his chinne, readie still to slop into his foming
chaps; ah, tis more than most intollerable.

speeches.speaker: Pier.
prose:
Nay faith, sweete neece, I was mightie strong
in thought we should haue shut vp night with an ould
Comedie: the Prince of Millane shall haue Mellida, &
thou shouldst haue

speeches.speaker: Ros.
prose:
No bodie, good sweete vncle. I tell you, sir, I
haue 39. seruants, and my munkey that makes the fortieth.
Now I loue al of them lightly for something, but
affect none of them seriously for any thing. One's a
passionate foole, and hee flatters mee aboue beliefe:
the second's a teastie ape, and hee railes at me beyond
reason: the third's as graue as some Censor, and hee
strokes vp his mustachoes three times, and makes six

plots of set faces, before he speakes one wise word: the
fourth's as dry, as the burre of an heartichoke; the fifth
paints, and hath alwaies a good colour for what hee
speakes: the sixt

speeches.speaker: Pie.
prose:
Stay, stay, sweet neece, what makes you thus suspect
young gallants worth.

speeches.speaker: Ross.
prose:
Oh, when I see one were a perewig, I dreade his
haire; another wallowe in a greate sloppe, I mistrust
the proportion of his thigh; and wears a ruffled boot,
I feare the fashion of his legge. Thus, something in each
thing, one tricke in euery thing makes me mistrust imperfection
in all parts; and there's the full point of my
addiction.

speeches.speaker: Pier.
verse: The roome's too scant: boyes, stand in there, close.

speeches.speaker: Mel.
verse: In faith, faire sir, I am too sad to daunce.

speeches.speaker: Pie.
verse: How's that, how's that? too sad? By heauen dance,
And grace him to, or, goe to, I say no more.

speeches.speaker: Mell.
verse: A burning glasse, the word splendente Phoebo?
Tis too curious, I conceipt it not.

speeches.speaker: Gal.
verse: I doe not dote vpon your excellence.
And faith, vnlesse you shed your brightest beames
Of sunny fauour, and acceptiue grace
Vpon my tender loue, I doe not burne:
prose:
Faith, ile tel thee. Ile no longer burne, then youle
shine and smile vpon my loue. For looke yee fairest, by
your pure sweets,

Marry but shine, and ile reflect your beames,

with feruent ardor. Faith I wold be loath to flatter thee
faire soule, because I loue, not doat, court like thy husband;
which thy father sweares, to morrowe morne I
must be. This is all, and now from henceforth, trust me
Mellida, Ile not speake one wise word to thee more.

speeches.speaker: Mell.
prose: I trust yee.

speeches.speaker: Gal.
prose: By my troth, Ile speak pure foole to thee now.

speeches.speaker: Mel.
prose: You will speake the liker your selfe.

speeches.speaker: Gal.
prose:
Good faith, Ile accept of the cockescombe, so
you will not refuse the bable.

speeches.speaker: Mel.
prose:
Nay good sweet, keepe them both, I am enamour'd
of neither.

speeches.speaker: Gal.
prose:
Goe to, I must take you downe for this. Lende
me your eare.

speeches.speaker: Ros.
prose: A glowe worme, the word? Splendescit tantùm tenebris.

speeches.speaker: Matz.
prose:
O, Ladie, the glowe worme figurates my valour:
which shineth brightest in most darke, dismall and horrid
atchieuements.

speeches.speaker: Ross.
prose:
Or rather, your glowe worme represents your
wit, which only seems to haue fire in it, though indeed
tis but an ignis fatuus, and shines onely in the darke
deade night of fooles admiration.

speeches.speaker: Matz.
prose:
Ladie, my wit hath spurs, if it wete dispos'd to
ride you.

speeches.speaker: Ross.
prose:
Faith sir, your wits spurs haue but walking rowels;
dull, blunt, they will not drawe blood: the gentlemen
vshers may admit them the Presence, for anie
wrong they can doe to Ladies.

speeches.speaker: Bal.
Fla.
prose:
Though you are mask't, I can guesse who you
are by your wit. You are not the exquisite Balurdo, the
most rarely shap't Balurdo.

speeches.speaker: Ba.
prose:
Who, I? No I am not sir Ieffrey Balurdo. I am not
as well knowne by my wit, as an alehouse by a red lattice.
I am not worthy to loue and be belou'd of Flauia.

speeches.speaker: Fla.
prose:
I will not scorne to fauour such good parts, as
are applauded in your rarest selfe.

speeches.speaker: Bal.
prose:
Truely, you speake wisely, and like a Iantlewoman
of foureteene yeares of age. You know the stone
called lapis; the nearer it comes to the fire, the hotter
it is: and the bird, which the Geometricians cal Auis,
the farther it is from the earth, the nearer it is to the
heauen: and loue, the nigher it is to the flame, the
more remote (ther's a word, remote) the more remote
it is from the frost, Your wit is quicke, a little thinge
pleaseth a young Ladie, and a smal fauour contenteth
an ould Courtier; and so, sweete mistresse I trusse my
codpeece point.

speeches.speaker: Pier.
prose: What might import this florish? bring vs word.

speeches.speaker: Fel.
prose:
Stand away: here's such a companie of flibotes,
hulling about this galleasse of greatnesse, that there's
no boarding him.
Doe you heare yon thing call'd, Duke?

speeches.speaker: Pie.
prose: How now blunt Feliche, what's the newes?

speeches.speaker: Fel.
prose:
Yonder's a knight, hath brought Andrugio's
head, & craues admittance to your chaire of state.

speeches.speaker: Pie.
verse: Conduct him with attendance sumptuous,
Sound all the pleasing instruments of ioy:
Make tryumph, stand on tiptoe whil'st wee meete:
O sight most gratious, O reuenge most sweete!

speeches.speaker: And.
prose:
We vowe, by the honour of our birth, to recompence
any man that brngeth Andrugio's head, with twentie thousand
double Pistolets, and the endeering to our choysest loue.

speeches.speaker: Pie.
verse: We still with most vnmou'd resolu'd confirme
Our large munificence: and here breath
A sad and solemne protestation:
When I recall this vowe, O, let our house
Be euen commaunded, staind, and trampled on,
As worthlesse rubbish of nobilitie.

speeches.speaker: And.
verse: Then, here, Piero, is Andrugios head,
Royally casked in a helme of steele:
Giue me thy loue, and take it. My dauntlesse soule
Hath that vnbounded vigor in his spirits,
